sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: The Picasso bug is a true bug, a close cousin of stink bugs, wearing an oversized dome-shaped shell (a scutellum) that covers its entire back like a hard-shell suitcase, patterned in swirling bands of turquoise, black, cream, and orange with no two patterns quite alike. It's found across Sub-Saharan Africa, and Kenya is its best-documented home — roughly a third of all confirmed sightings anywhere in the world come from Kenya alone, more than double any other single country.

sections.heading: What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: A rounded, strongly domed, shield-like body resembling a tiny ornate turtle shell, with bold swirling colour bands earning the 'Picasso' nickname. The oversized back-shield (scutellum) covers the whole abdomen and both pairs of wings underneath, a feature that gives this family its 'jewel bug' name. No rigorous scientific description of exactly how big this species gets, or how males and females differ, could be found in the authoritative sources checked.

sections.heading: How Does It Live?
sections.body: The detailed life story of this species — egg count, nymph stages, breeding season — isn't nailed down anywhere in citable, checkable research; much of what's repeated online traces back to unverified, crowd-edited sources rather than real research. A close relative in the same family is known to practice genuine maternal care, guarding her egg mass and newly hatched young (removing her causes near-total nymphal death within days) — whether Picasso bugs do the same hasn't been confirmed, but it's a trait that shows up across the family.

sections.heading: Where Does It Live, and What Does It Eat?
sections.body: In Kenya, it's known to feed on avocado flowers, piercing them to drink the plant's sap — a bad infestation can be intense enough to slow the tree's growth, which matters to Kenya's large avocado farming industry. Popular sources claim it feeds on cotton, coffee, and citrus too, but none of that could be confirmed against real scientific or government sources, so it's left out here rather than repeated as fact.

sections.heading: Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: Where it shows up on farms it's treated as a minor pest, mainly of avocado flowers in Kenya. But it's worth remembering a species can be scientifically fascinating without being economically dramatic — this one's real claim to fame is its stunning good looks and its surprisingly murky taxonomic history.

sections.heading: A Scientific Plot Twist
sections.body: For a long time, insects like this were assumed to belong to a particular subgroup of jewel bugs, but a detailed 2018 genetic study sequencing DNA across the whole jewel bug family found the Picasso bug's true relatives are different from what was long assumed, placing it in a different branch of the family tree. The formal global scientific name also carries no subspecies, while Kenyan agricultural records refer to it with an extra name tacked on — a small mismatch between museum taxonomy and on-the-ground naming.

sections.heading: What's the Kenya Connection?
sections.body: Kenya isn't just somewhere this species happens to occur — it's the single best-documented country for it anywhere on Earth based on confirmed observation records, and it's also tracked there as a known avocado pest by Kenya's own agricultural research organisation. Most people who spot its dazzling shell on a leaf have no idea it's practically a local celebrity.

sections.heading: What Are Wolf Spiders?
sections.body: Wolf spiders are widespread, ancient ground-dwelling hunters that actively chase down prey on foot rather than sitting in a web — solitary predators found on every continent except Antarctica. There are roughly 2,400 known species in the family Lycosidae across about 120 genera, ranging from barely a centimetre long to several centimetres in the large genus Hogna; despite their fearsome reputation, they are entirely harmless to people.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Typically brown, grey, or sandy for ground camouflage, stocky, hairy, and fast-moving. The real giveaway is their eyes: four small eyes in a bottom row, two large forward-facing eyes in the middle, and two even larger eyes on top of the head — a three-row arrangement giving genuinely good vision most spiders lack. The body divides into a front cephalothorax (legs, eyes, mouthparts) and a rounder rear abdomen holding the silk-spinning spinnerets.

sections.heading: The Eyes Have It — Night Hunting with Built-In Torches
sections.body: A mirror-like reflective layer behind the rear eyes (the tapetum lucidum, the same structure behind a cat's glowing eyes) makes wolf spiders' eyes blaze back green or amber under torchlight at night, letting experienced collectors simply spot and harvest them by eye. This amplifies dim light and dramatically improves their ability to detect prey and predators in near-darkness.

sections.heading: Life as a Hunter
sections.body: Wolf spiders don't build webs to catch prey; they wander the ground through leaf litter, soil, and grass, actively stalking or ambushing insects, beetles, ants, and small grasshoppers. Some genera (Hogna, Geolycosa) dig burrows as a daytime retreat; others are fully nomadic. In farmland they are one of the most important natural pest controllers, significantly suppressing aphids and other damaging insects in rice, wheat, and other crops.

sections.heading: The Dancing Mama — Maternal Care Unique in the Spider World
sections.body: After mating, the female spins a silk egg sac and attaches it to her spinnerets, carrying it beneath her abdomen everywhere she goes and never putting it down. When the eggs hatch, dozens of spiderlings climb onto her back and ride there for days to weeks. This dorsal-carrying behaviour is found nowhere else among the world's roughly 40,000 spider species — it's exclusive to Lycosidae.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Wolf spiders are ecologically flexible, thriving in grasslands, forest floors, sandy deserts, high-altitude scree, wetland margins, farmland, and city gardens and pavements. Several Pardosa species are especially comfortable in urban environments, sometimes wandering into ground-floor rooms.

sections.heading: Are They Dangerous?
sections.body: No — their venom has no medically significant effect on humans; a rare, defensive bite may cause brief local pain comparable to a wasp sting with no lasting effects. The famous medieval 'tarantula of Taranto,' blamed for a supposed dancing madness, was in fact a large wolf spider (Hogna radiata), not a true tarantula — the panic was cultural, not medical.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Beyond pest control, wolf spiders (particularly the genus Pardosa) are widely used by scientists as bioindicators — a healthy, diverse wolf spider population signals a clean, ecologically intact habitat, and their sensitivity to soil contamination and pesticides makes them valuable environmental monitors.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Giant water bugs are true bugs (order Hemiptera, family Belostomatidae) — not beetles, not flies — with a piercing, straw-like mouthpart repurposed into a venom-injecting stiletto capable of rapidly liquefying the insides of a frog. The family is ancient, with fossils appearing in the Triassic some 245 million years ago, contemporaries of the first dinosaurs.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The family spans from fingernail-length to genuine giants over 11 centimetres, the largest true bugs on Earth. The body is broadly oval and flattened like a domed shield, typically brown with pale margins; front legs are heavy, hooked, and raptorial for snatching prey, while the middle and hind legs are fringed with hairs and used as paddles. Most East African species (genus Appasus) are medium-sized, sturdy, palm-filling bugs.

sections.heading: What Do They Hunt?
sections.body: Almost anything they can overpower: tadpoles, small fish, aquatic insects, and frogs are standard prey, with larger species documented killing snakes and reportedly seizing small birds. They inject a cocktail of hydrolytic enzymes and paralysing toxins through their proboscis, then wait for prey to liquefy before drinking the result. One African genus, Limnogeton, specialises exclusively on freshwater snails and has lost its grasping forelegs entirely.

sections.heading: The Strangest Family in Entomology
sections.body: A male giant water bug carries up to 150 fertilised eggs glued across his back and spends a week doing almost nothing else but repeatedly exposing them to air and sweeping oxygenated water over the clutch — remove the eggs and every one dies within hours. This mandatory full-time paternal care is found in fewer than 100 of the roughly one million known insect species. Females glue eggs directly to the male's wing covers, remating with him after every few eggs so sperm precedence guarantees his paternity — one recorded male copulated 100 times in 36 hours while 144 eggs were laid.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Giant water bugs occur on every continent except Antarctica, most abundantly in the tropics; in East Africa and tropical Asia, medium-sized genera like Appasus and Diplonychus are common in shallow ponds, rice paddies, and slow streams. Adults are strong fliers, disperse at night, and are drawn irresistibly to artificial lights — 'electric light bug' is a common name in parts of Africa.

sections.heading: Do People Eat Them?
sections.body: In Thailand, the large Asian species Lethocerus indicus is a prized food, roasted, fried, or steamed, with males selling for three to four times the price of females because of a fragrant abdominal secretion used as the essential flavouring in nam prik mangda, a relish served as a dip or rice topping. In parts of Indochina, giant water bugs rank alongside crickets and grasshoppers as everyday edible insects.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: As top invertebrate predators they help structure freshwater food webs, and the asynchronous flight muscles of the giant genus Lethocerus became one of the primary model systems for understanding how insect muscles contract. On the applied side, large belostomatids are occasional fish-hatchery pests, while the snail-specialist Limnogeton is a potential ally against the snails that host the parasite causing schistosomiasis, a widespread disease in sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Amegilla, commonly known as the blue-banded bee or digger bee, is a solitary bee that digs her own burrow in bare, sun-baked clay soil and raises her young alone, never living in a hive or sharing a nest. There are more than 250 species in the genus worldwide, with at least a dozen documented in Kenya, including Amegilla vivida, only confirmed in the country for the first time in 2019.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Bands of pale, metallic-blue or silvery hair run across an otherwise dark, fuzzy abdomen. In the best-studied species, males come in two dramatically different sizes, some rivalling the largest females, driven by fierce competition over mates.

sections.heading: How Do They Dig a Nest — With Spit?
sections.body: Females target flat, rock-hard clay and soften it first with nectar before excavating, building a mud 'chimney' turret around the entrance that she later demolishes. Rather than packing solid pollen balls, she leaves her larva a pool of liquid food; once fed, the larva can go dormant for eight to ten years, and scientists don't fully understand what triggers it to finally pupate.

sections.heading: Why Is Their Buzzing So Special?
sections.body: Some flowers, including tomato, eggplant, and the rare African violet, hide pollen inside pores that only vibration can release, a trick called buzz pollination; studies show eggplants pollinated by Amegilla produce heavier fruit with more seeds. One species, Amegilla vivida, goes further in Central Africa, triggering a spring-loaded 'explosive pollination' mechanism in certain rainforest flowers.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Amegilla is an Old World genus found across Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia, with Australia and South Africa holding the largest populations; at least a dozen species are recorded in Kenya, including Amegilla kaimosica, named for the town of Kaimosi. In the Taita Hills, four Amegilla species are the only known pollinators of the critically endangered African violet Saintpaulia teitensis.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Amegilla needs only bare clay soil and nearby flowers to thrive, making her a free pollination workforce for crops including coriander in Turkana, watermelon and pigeon pea in Kenya, cowpea in Cameroon, and greenhouse tomatoes in Australia. Because she is vulnerable to pesticides, researchers in Cameroon have tested gentler, plant-based insecticides to keep her undisturbed while foraging on cowpea flowers.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: A larva can stay dormant for up to a decade before becoming an adult, for reasons still not fully understood. Cuckoo bees in the genus Thyreus sneak into sealed Amegilla nest cells to lay eggs on the stolen food, and some males are so much larger than others of their own species that they could be mistaken for a different species entirely.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: The blue-banded bee builds and provisions her own nest without a hive or colony, softening hard clay with nectar and shaking pollen loose from flowers other bees cannot unlock. She quietly supports crops and rare wildflowers across Kenya and beyond, one solitary burrow at a time.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Antlions belong to the family Myrmeleontidae within the order Neuroptera, which also includes lacewings and owlflies; the order has almost 6,000 species worldwide, with the antlion family alone accounting for more than 1,600, the largest family in the group. Antlions occur on every continent except Antarctica, with the greatest variety in Africa, Asia, and Australia.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults resemble damselflies, with long lacy wings, a slender abdomen, and club-shaped antennae; most have wingspans of 4-8 cm, though the tribe Palparini can reach 17 cm. The larva looks completely different: a squat, bristly, sand-coloured oval with hollow, curved jaws used to stab, inject venom, and drink prey, producing no solid waste until it pupates.

sections.heading: How Do They Hunt?
sections.body: Roughly 70% of antlion species never build a pit trap, instead lying buried just beneath the sand surface and detecting prey vibrations before lunging upward. Pit-building species excavate a conical pit about 5 cm wide and deep by flicking sand with their heads, then lie in wait at the bottom; when prey slides in and tries to escape, they flick sand to trigger avalanches before striking with venom-injecting jaws.

sections.heading: Growing Up — From Pit to Pupa to Adult
sections.body: Larval development typically takes more than a year, sometimes several years, through three growth stages with progressively bigger pits. The larva spins a silk cocoon using its Malpighian tubules (excretory organs) rather than mouth glands, making it nearly unique among silk producers; the pupa can remain dormant for up to six years before the adult emerges.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Antlions need loose, dry, sandy soil, found in sheltered spots such as under rocks, tree canopies, ruins, and bridges, mostly in arid and semi-arid landscapes. The Afrotropical Region is the most diverse on Earth for the lacewing group, and the giant tribe Palparini has its centre of diversity in southern Africa, where 45 of its 100 species occur, 35 of them found nowhere else.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: All antlion larvae are predators of ants, beetles, and other ground-dwelling invertebrates, making them natural population regulators. Their pit-building behaviour has been studied for decades as a model for foraging strategy and decision-making, and in parts of Africa antlion larvae have traditionally been used in folk medicine and divination.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: The largest antlions (tribe Palparini, up to 17 cm wingspan) are confined mainly to Africa and Asia, absent from Australia and North America. The larva paralyses prey with venom, liquefies its insides, drinks the resulting fluid, then flicks out the empty husk and resets the trap; adults are powerful nocturnal fliers rarely seen except at lit windows.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: Antlions have evolved two different prey-catching strategies (the pit trap and the vibration-sensing ambush), produce silk from their kidneys, can remain dormant as pupae for years, and give rise to damselfly-like adults. The family ranges from small generalists to spectacular 17 cm giants across southern Africa.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Assassin bugs are an entire family, Reduviidae, with 6,800-7,000 known species that stab prey with a needle-like beak, inject a liquefying cocktail, and drink the results. The photographed nymph, with its bright red body and black head and legs, belongs to the family's largest branch, Harpactorinae (about 2,000 species), but nymphs cannot be pinned to an exact species from a photo alone.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The family's giveaway is a ridged sound-producing groove on the underside of the chest, a long narrow 'neck,' and a curved needle-like beak folded beneath the head; sizes range from 4 cm giants to 2-3 mm specks, with most adults drab but many nymphs bold red-and-black. They hatch as wingless miniature adults and pass through about five nymph stages before their final molt into a winged adult.

sections.heading: How Does It Hunt?
sections.body: Most assassin bugs are ambush predators that grab prey with their front legs and drive in a needle-beak, injecting enzyme-laden saliva that dissolves the victim's insides before drinking the liquefied meal. One African species disguises its nymphs with a 'backpack' of up to 20 dead ant carcasses, proven at Lake Victoria to fool sight-hunting jumping spiders, while two other species studied near Mbita Point specialise in hunting jumping spiders themselves.

sections.heading: Why Should You Be Careful?
sections.body: The needle-beak can pierce human skin and, by documented account, causes sharp immediate pain and swelling; one case report describes itching lasting two weeks with full recovery within three weeks. A related subfamily, Triatominae or 'kissing bugs,' feeds on blood and spreads Chagas disease in the Americas, but a 2025 global survey found essentially no established populations anywhere in East Africa, and the pictured ambush-predator nymph is not one of them.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Assassin bugs are valuable to farmers; in West Africa two species were observed preying on fall armyworm caterpillars, a serious maize pest across the region including Kenya, and in Benin another species measurably reduced damage to stored yam chips. Researchers in India mass-rear an assassin bug species for release onto cotton fields as pest control, and while there is no documented Kenya-specific release programme yet, Kenya hosts nearly 500 recorded assassin bug sightings, several from a genus already proven useful as biocontrol elsewhere.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: The 'horrid king assassin bug' produces venom combining prey-killing, antimicrobial, and tissue-breaking functions, and a related species secretes venom from three separate glandular chambers each with a specialised job. Assassin bugs also make sound using the ridged chest groove and beak tip, though exactly what the sound is used for in the wild remains an open question.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: The assassin bug family combines patient ambush hunting with a chemical weapon disguised as a drinking straw, including at least two Kenyan species that hunt spiders instead of insects. The red-and-black nymph photographed belongs to the family's largest branch and is likely already stalking its next meal.

sections.heading: 1. What Is the Banana Fly?
sections.body: The banana fly belongs to the family Neriidae, a small tropical group of 183 known species called banana stalk flies or cactus flies, poorly studied enough that no major entomology textbook devotes a chapter to it. It sits alongside the stilt-legged flies (Micropezidae), a sister family sharing its most distinctive trait, disproportionately long legs.

sections.heading: 2. What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: The fly has stilt-like legs, a yellow-orange abdomen with dark banding, large compound eyes, and wings held flat over its back at rest. A visible droplet at the mouthparts is a regurgitation feeding trick well-documented in its close relatives the Micropezidae, and like all flies it has halteres, club-shaped organs that act as gyroscopes during flight.

sections.heading: 3. Where Does It Fit in the Fly Family Tree?
sections.body: Diptera contains over 154,000 described species; the banana fly sits within the Schizophora ('higher flies') and the Acalyptratae subsection, distinguished by the absence of a calypter wing lobe. Within Acalyptratae it belongs to the superfamily Nerioidea, a small cluster of three families (Neriidae, Micropezidae, Tanypezidae) alongside other acalyptrate groups such as the fruit-fly family Tephritidae.

sections.heading: 4. An Honest Gap in the Books
sections.body: A systematic search of sixteen major entomological reference books found that Neriidae appears only in species-count tables and phylogenetic diagrams, with no textbook devoting even a paragraph to its biology, behaviour, or ecology. This is not unusual for small, tropical families whose natural history is known mainly to specialists working from primary literature and fieldwork.

sections.heading: 5. Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: The banana fly belongs to Diptera, an order that one major textbook says 'clearly surpasses all other insect orders in economic and medical impact,' as flies transmit diseases, pollinate crops, recycle organic matter, and serve as key model organisms in genetics. The banana fly itself is not a significant pest or disease vector, but it shares its superfamily with the stilt-legged flies whose long-legged, leaf-surface lifestyle closely mirrors its own.

sections.heading: 1. What Are Biting Midges?
sections.body: Biting midges are among the smallest flies on Earth, some just 0.5-3 mm long, often called 'no-see-ums.' About 4,000 species are known worldwide, and DNA testing has shown that midges once thought to be a single species can turn out to be three distinct ones, which matters because only one of the three may transmit livestock disease.

sections.heading: 2. What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults have a robust, slightly hump-backed shape at rest, with wings often patterned in dark and light spots and folded flat over the back; only females have piercing, blood-sucking mouthparts, while males have fuzzy feather-like antennae used to find swarms of females. Larvae are slender, legless, worm-like swimmers, and pupae float to the surface to breathe but rapidly paddle downward when disturbed.

sections.heading: 3. Incredible Feats and Strange Biology
sections.body: One type of midge holds the record for the fastest wingbeat of any insect, over 1,000 beats per second, achieved through 'asynchronous' muscles that click automatically. Some larvae can survive being almost completely dried out through cryptobiosis, and females that don't get enough blood will reabsorb their own undeveloped eggs.

sections.heading: 4. Where Do They Live and What Do They Do?
sections.body: Larvae need moisture and are found in pond-edge mud, marshes, water-filled tree holes, rotting fruit, and wet soil, often being the first 'pioneer' insects to colonize new tropical rainwater puddles. Midges also thrive in the Arctic, where massive summer swarms harass caribou and reindeer, and one group is the exclusive pollinator of the cacao tree, without which there would be no chocolate.

sections.heading: 5. Medical and Veterinary Concerns
sections.body: Beyond itchy bites, midges are major vectors of Bluetongue Virus and African Horse Sickness, serious diseases affecting sheep, cattle, goats, and horses. Across East Africa, where pastoralism underpins millions of livelihoods, these midge-borne diseases pose an ongoing threat capable of devastating herds.

sections.heading: 6. How Are They Controlled?
sections.body: Standard mosquito window screens are too coarse to stop midges, requiring extra-fine mesh, and DEET sprays offer only temporary protection. Livestock owners manage midges by eliminating standing water and wet manure, while farmers use light traps to monitor populations and vaccines to protect animals from midge-borne viruses.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: The bee in the photograph belongs to Thyreus, nicknamed 'domino cuckoo bees,' members of the family Apidae (the same family as honeybees and bumblebees) that never build a nest or collect pollen for their own young. Instead, they sneak into another bee's nursery and let that bee do all the work, exactly like the cuckoo bird they're named after.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Thyreus has a jet-black body with patches of dense white feather-like hairs on the face, thorax sides, and legs, plus white spots along the abdomen edges, and smoky or blue-tinted wings held flat against the body. Females lack pollen baskets on their legs entirely, since they never provision a nest of their own.

sections.heading: How Does the 'Cuckoo' Trick Work?
sections.body: A female cuckoo bee waits until a host bee has provisioned and sealed a brood cell, then breaks in, lays her own egg on the stockpiled food, and in some cases her larva also destroys the host's egg or grub. The main hosts are digger bees in the genus Amegilla, with some Thyreus species specializing on Anthophora instead; confirming which cuckoo bee parasitizes which host requires watching an actual nest, not just seeing both flying near the same flowers.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Thyreus is an Old World genus found across Africa, Europe, Asia, the Arabian Peninsula, and Australia, tracking its host Amegilla bees; researchers recognize roughly 108-115 species worldwide, about 50 of them in Africa. In Kenya, the host Amegilla vivida was only confirmed in 2019, and its documented parasite Thyreus pictus likely occurs there too, though a Kenyan specimen record hasn't yet turned up, despite one being catalogued just across the border in Ethiopia.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Cuckoo bees act as a natural population check on their host bees, similar to a hawk or wolf, since every successfully raised cuckoo bee generation means fewer host offspring survive. Because Thyreus depends entirely on its host doing well, it also serves as a biological indicator tied to the fortunes of pollinators that matter economically and ecologically, including the survival of a plant found nowhere else on Earth.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: Individual species carry names like the 'Neon Cuckoo Bee,' 'Chequered Cuckoo Bee,' and 'Domino Cuckoo Bee.' Many Thyreus species look nearly identical, and telling them apart often requires examining male genital structures under a microscope, with one paper calling the genus 'a bane of melittologists'; the shield-shaped plate on its thorax has also drawn research interest for studying how genes control body shape.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: The cuckoo bee survives entirely by breaking into another bee's sealed pantry rather than building its own, stripped of pollen-gathering tools but dressed in dazzling white-on-black colouring. Its fortunes rise and fall with the hardworking digger bees it depends on.

sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: Dicercomyzon, the fringed-sucker clinger, is a mayfly in the ancient order Ephemeroptera, placed in the family Oligoneuriidae, a worldwide group of about 54 species in 13 genera absent only from Australia and New Zealand. Its common name reflects its ability to cling in fast water and the fringed forelegs it uses to filter food from the current.

sections.heading: What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: The nymph is dorsoventrally flattened with a pale body, robust gripping legs, and three trailing tails (two cerci and a central filament), typical of fast-water mayflies. Its most distinctive feature is fringed forelegs held outstretched into the current as a filter-feeding sieve, plus gill plates along the abdomen that absorb dissolved oxygen and beat faster when levels drop; the adult, if it follows the standard mayfly pattern, would have large triangular forewings and much smaller or absent hindwings.

sections.heading: How Does a Mayfly Live?
sections.body: The nymph lives its entire substantive life underwater, lasting from a few weeks to three years and moulting 15 to 50 times, while the adult stage is almost an afterthought. It surfaces and moults into a subimago, a pre-adult flying stage unique to mayflies, then moults once more into the true adult (imago), which does not eat, has only hours to days to mate, and dies after eggs are laid.

sections.heading: The Fringed Forelegs — A Filter-Feeding Trick
sections.body: Unlike most mayfly nymphs, which scrape algae from rock surfaces with their jaws, Oligoneuriidae nymphs including Dicercomyzon hold their forelegs into the current like nets, using dense hair fringes to capture microscopic organic particles. This is a rare feeding strategy among mayflies, actively harvesting the energy of flowing water rather than just clinging to rock.

sections.heading: Where Do Mayflies Live, and How Many Are There?
sections.body: Mayflies occur on every continent except Antarctica in a wide variety of freshwater habitats, with more than 3,000 species across around 40 families; Oligoneuriidae has 54 known species worldwide, absent from Australia and New Zealand. Specific range data for Dicercomyzon itself are not detailed in the major reference texts, but the group favours clean, fast-flowing tropical and subtropical rivers, and the order dates back to definitive fossils from roughly 290 million years ago.

sections.heading: Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: Mayfly nymphs are a cornerstone of freshwater food webs, converting algae and organic particles into biomass that feeds invertebrates, fish, frogs, and waterfowl, and they are highly valued as indicators of river health since they are sensitive to pollution and habitat degradation. Mayfly density has been shown to drop by 62% in streams with less than 30 metres of intact riparian forest, and mass emergences of some species have piled up on roads and bridges over a metre deep.

sections.heading: A Note on the Name
sections.body: Dicercomyzon is sometimes listed under the family name Dicercomyzidae in regional and field literature, reflecting ongoing revisions to mayfly taxonomy. The most recent large-scale reference works place it within Oligoneuriidae, alongside related genera such as Machadorythus, as taxonomy at this level continues to evolve with DNA analysis.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Marsh beetles belong to the family Scirtidae, previously known as Helodidae, a worldwide family of about 600 to 700 species found mostly in temperate regions of the northern hemisphere. Adults live in vegetation bordering ponds and marshes, while the larvae are fully aquatic, living in still ponds, swamps, and sometimes rotting logs.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The larva is the most distinctive stage: flat, ribbon-like, broadened side to side, with long antennae, banded pale-and-dark segments, and fine bristles. Adults are more conventional, small, nondescript beetles that blend into waterside vegetation.

sections.heading: How Do They Breathe Underwater?
sections.body: Marsh beetle larvae use two respiratory strategies at once: anal gills that absorb dissolved oxygen directly from the water, and a plastron — a microscopic air layer trapped by water-repelling hairs that continually refills itself as dissolved oxygen diffuses in. This dual system gives the larvae unusual flexibility compared with most aquatic insects.

sections.heading: What Do They Eat?
sections.body: Larvae are filter feeders, sifting still water and substrate for algae, diatoms, fungal threads, and decomposing organic matter, aided by a specialised grinding pad (mola) on the mandibles. This places them as microscopic recyclers that move energy from the bottom of the food web upward.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Larvae are confined to still or slow-moving water such as ponds, swamps, and vegetated lake margins, unlike aquatic beetle families that colonise fast rivers. Adults stay on plants bordering the pond or marsh where they emerged.

sections.heading: How Many Species Are There, and Where?
sections.body: About 600 to 700 species are known worldwide, on every continent except Antarctica, with greatest diversity in temperate wetland regions; 254 species in 8 genera are recorded in the Palearctic region alone. The family's placement within the beetle order remains debated among taxonomists using anatomical and DNA evidence.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Marsh beetles are not pests and do not bite, sting, or carry disease. By grazing algae and recycling organic debris, larvae help keep still-water ecosystems from becoming stagnant and convert microscopic productivity into food available to fish, waterfowl, and other wetland animals.

sections.heading: 1. What Are Mealybugs?
sections.body: Mealybugs are small, sap-sucking insects, typically 2 to 7 mm long, related to scale insects and aphids, and among the most economically damaging plant pests worldwide. About 2,000 species have been described, attacking orchards, sugarcane, forest trees, greenhouse crops, and houseplants, and they spread globally because they are small and easily overlooked in traded plants.

sections.heading: 2. What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Females are soft, oval, wingless insects covered in a powdery or filamentous white wax; some, like the longtailed mealybug, trail wax threads as long as their body. Males resemble tiny flies with one pair of wings, no functional mouthparts, and live only a few days, while the mobile 'crawler' nymph stage is chiefly responsible for spreading infestations.

sections.heading: 3. Extraordinary Biology
sections.body: Male mealybugs undergo a butterfly-like transformation through a prepupa and pupa before becoming winged adults, unlike most insects in their group that simply moult in stages. Females retain juvenile, wingless traits into adulthood and can even reabsorb developing eggs to conserve energy when conditions are poor.

sections.heading: 4. How They Damage Plants — and Why Ants Love Them
sections.body: Mealybugs pierce plant tissue and suck sap, and heavy infestations can weaken or kill a plant; some species also inject toxins or transmit viruses. The sugary honeydew they excrete promotes sooty mould growth and attracts ants, which tend mealybug colonies and drive off the predators and parasitic wasps that would otherwise control them.

sections.heading: 5. When a Bug Threatens Food Security
sections.body: In the 1970s the cassava mealybug, accidentally introduced from South America, devastated cassava harvests across Africa, a staple crop for about 200 million people including coastal Kenya and Tanzania. A parasitic wasp from Paraguay eventually brought the outbreak under control, but only after an initial misidentification of the mealybug species delayed the correct match between pest and wasp.

sections.heading: 6. The Beetle That Founded a Whole Field of Science
sections.body: In 1888 the cottony-cushion scale, a mealybug relative, was devastating California's citrus industry until entomologist Charles Riley imported the vedalia beetle from Australia, which virtually eliminated the pest within two years for under US$5,000. This introduction is now regarded as the founding moment of classical biological control, underscoring that precise species identification and natural enemies can be highly effective.

sections.heading: 1. What Are Pond Skaters?
sections.body: Pond skaters, also called water striders, Jesus bugs, or wherrymen, are true bugs of the family Gerridae (order Hemiptera) that walk and sprint across water without getting wet; the tropical genus Limnogonus is among the most widespread, found across Africa, Asia, Australia, and the Americas. There are roughly 620 to 700 species worldwide on every continent except the polar regions, and a related genus, Halobates, lives permanently on the open ocean.

sections.heading: 2. What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: They have a long, narrow, dark body and enormously long middle and hind legs that spread out wide, while short front legs are held forward to grab prey. Water-repelling pegs and pores on their feet let the legs dimple the surface without piercing it; males are generally smaller than females, and some species show elaborate courtship structures or female defensive spines.

sections.heading: 3. How Do They Walk on Water?
sections.body: Pond skaters exploit surface tension by spreading their weight across six long, water-repellent legs that press lightly on the water film without breaking it. Middle legs row like oars, hind legs steer like a rudder, and short front legs are held ready to grab prey.

sections.heading: 4. What Do They Eat?
sections.body: Pond skaters are predators that detect ripples from insects and other small creatures struggling on the water surface, then row over, pin the prey with their front legs, and pierce and suck it dry with beak-like mouthparts. There is also some evidence they occasionally take small aquatic crustaceans from just below the surface.

sections.heading: 5. How Do They Talk to Each Other?
sections.body: Pond skaters communicate through species-specific ripple patterns tapped or vibrated onto the water surface, a channel with no real parallel among other insects, which typically use sound, scent, or light. Males produce calling signals that convey different messages, and females can read and respond to them.

sections.heading: 6. How Do They Reproduce?
sections.body: Courtship is often contested, with females frequently resisting mating, making pond skaters a celebrated example of sexual conflict; eggs are then laid in rows on plant stems or objects at the water's edge. Young hatch wingless and pass through five instars with no pupal stage, and whether an adult develops wings can depend on genetics and on whether its habitat is permanent or seasonal.

sections.heading: 7. Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Limnogonus and most pond skaters prefer still or slow-moving fresh water such as ponds, ditches, and calm stream margins in the tropics and subtropics. Some relatives, the ocean-going Halobates, live fully on the open sea, and fossils show this marine lifestyle dates back at least 45 million years.

sections.heading: 8. Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Pond skaters link land and water in the food web by consuming terrestrial insects that fall onto ponds, and their sensitivity to pollution makes their presence a useful indicator of water quality. They are also heavily studied in animal behaviour research on sexual conflict, since counter-adaptations in females provide clear evidence of an evolutionary arms race between the sexes.

sections.heading: 9. Surprising Facts
sections.body: The name 'Jesus bugs' reflects their water-walking ability; unlike most water-repellent insects, their feet use a unique pattern of pegs and pores rather than hairs. A 45-million-year-old Halobates fossil from Verona, Italy shows ocean-going pond skaters once lived in the Mediterranean, and Halobates remains the only insect genus living permanently on the open ocean, with five of its 45 species never touching land.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Red velvet mites are fuzzy, red, ball-shaped relatives of spiders and ticks; the giant species found across Kenya's drylands, often referred to as Dinothrombium, are the largest mites on Earth. They spend nearly their whole lives underground and erupt en masse once or twice a year, a phenomenon photographed across Kenya from Samburu and Wajir to Amboseli and the coast at Watamu over more than twenty years.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults reach up to about 1.4 centimetres long, the largest in their family, and are covered in dense red 'fur,' sometimes with white spots, over a tough, hard-to-puncture shell. Babies look nothing like adults — hatching with six legs as hitchhikers on other insects, while adults have eight legs and roam freely.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: An adult may spend 51 weeks a year underground and essentially dormant, then emerge in huge numbers within hours of the first heavy rain, timed to coincide with the mass flights of termites and ants, which the adults prey on for one to three days before returning underground. As larvae, red velvet mites are instead parasites, hitching rides on grasshoppers, beetles, moths, spiders, and sun spiders, and a single female can lay up to 100,000 eggs.

sections.heading: Why Are They Red?
sections.body: Their vivid red colour is a warning signal, and testing against 40 predator species found almost none would eat one twice. Their reportedly bitter, astringent, spicy taste and tough shell mean researchers describe them as having essentially no real predators, and injecting their body fluid into lab mice caused no poisoning, suggesting the defence is external rather than an internal toxin.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Red velvet mites are not pests; by feeding heavily on termites and ants right as those insects emerge in flight, they likely act as a seasonal check on those populations. Claims that people in parts of Africa eat giant red velvet mites as a seasonal treat come only from informal, non-scientific sources gathered during this research, so this is noted as an intriguing rumour rather than a confirmed fact.

sections.heading: What's the Kenya Connection?
sections.body: Red velvet mite emergences are a distinctly Kenyan phenomenon, with sightings recorded across Baringo, Samburu, Laikipia, Kajiado, Meru, Wajir, and Kitui, typically following the first rains. One record comes from a wildlife biodiversity survey run jointly by a conservancy trust and a research institute in the Masol and Pellow conservancies.

sections.heading: 1. What Are They?
sections.body: The robber fly genus Hyperechia is a group of large, hairy African flies that closely mimic carpenter bees in colour and hair pattern, yet are fierce ambush hunters that prey on the very bees they resemble. Robber flies belong to the large family Asilidae, with 5,000 to 7,400 known species worldwide found on every continent except Antarctica's ice-free zones.

sections.heading: 2. What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Hyperechia adults are about 18 millimetres long with a stout black body, a pale band across the thorax, and long yellowish-white facial hairs matching a carpenter bee's colouring; legs are black and bristly. Large eyes with a sharpened 'acute zone' give them the visual precision to track fast-moving insects in flight.

sections.heading: 3. How Do They Hunt (and Live)?
sections.body: Robber flies spend about 98% of their time sitting still on a perch before launching a precisely aimed strike, seizing prey with their legs and paralysing it with toxic saliva that also begins digesting it. Hyperechia waits near carpenter bee nest entrances to ambush adult bees, while its own larvae develop as parasites inside carpenter bee larvae, making it predator and parasite within the same life cycle.

sections.heading: 4. Why Does It Look Like a Bee?
sections.body: This is Batesian mimicry, in which a species resembles a dangerous or defended one for protection, a strategy several unrelated insects have evolved toward bees and wasps. Scientists have not confirmed the exact reason for Hyperechia's resemblance, but it may both deter predators and help the fly approach carpenter bees unnoticed; the related robber fly Laphria does something similar mimicking a bumblebee.

sections.heading: 5. Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Hyperechia is found across Africa alongside its carpenter bee hosts, favouring sunny spots and often occurring around buildings and human settlements, sometimes hunting insects at porch lights at night.

sections.heading: 6. Are They Good or Bad for Us?
sections.body: Robber flies are generally beneficial, preying on wasps, dragonflies, grasshoppers, and other flies to help keep insect populations in check; Hyperechia specifically helps limit carpenter bee numbers alongside the parasitic bee-fly Anthrax. No literature reviewed found evidence of robber flies causing economic damage or requiring pest control.

sections.heading: 7. Notable Facts
sections.body: Hyperechia's bee disguise matches body colour, band placement, and hair pattern in detail, and it will tackle prey as large as itself, including bees and wasps. Very little life-history research exists for Asilidae overall despite it being one of the largest fly families, and not all unusual-looking robber flies are bee mimics — some sand-dune populations have plain white bodies instead.

sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: The Saucer Bug is a flattened, oval freshwater ambush predator belonging to the family Naucoridae, the 'creeping water bugs'; the genus featured here, Laccocoris, is found across tropical Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Despite its plain brown appearance, it has snap-trap forelegs, a self-replenishing underwater air supply, and a memorable bite.

sections.heading: What Does It Look Like?
sections.body: Adults are 5 to 20 millimetres long, flattened and broadly oval, light to dark brown, with antennae so short they disappear beneath the head. Its most distinctive feature is a pair of massively thickened front legs with the tibia and tarsus fused into a curved claw, forming raptorial grasping arms used purely for seizing prey.

sections.heading: How Does It Breathe Underwater?
sections.body: The Saucer Bug carries a bubble of air beneath its wings that acts as a 'physical gill,' refilling itself as dissolved oxygen from the water diffuses in to replace what is consumed. Experiments found the related Naucoris needed to surface only 5 to 20 times per hour versus 50 to 150 times for a Backswimmer, and it paddles its hind legs to keep fresh water flowing over the bubble; some relatives instead carry a permanent plastron that never needs resurfacing.

sections.heading: How Does It Hunt?
sections.body: Saucer Bugs creep slowly through submerged plants and debris rather than swimming strongly, snapping their raptorial forelegs shut on small aquatic creatures such as insect larvae, crustaceans, and worms, then piercing and digesting prey externally. This places them near the top of the invertebrate food web in their pond or stream habitat.

sections.heading: Will It Bite Me?
sections.body: Yes — Saucer Bugs will bite in self-defence if handled or squeezed, and while not medically dangerous for most people, the bite is sharp and memorable.

sections.heading: Where Does It Live, and How Many Are There?
sections.body: Naucorids occur on every continent except Antarctica, in streams, lakes, ponds, springs, ditches, and garden pools, while the genus Laccocoris is concentrated in tropical Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. The family contains an estimated 391 to 500 described species across 37 to 40 genera, a count that has more than doubled from older estimates as tropical freshwater habitats have been more thoroughly surveyed.

sections.heading: Why Does It Matter?
sections.body: By preying on invertebrates, Saucer Bugs help regulate smaller insect populations, and because they are sensitive to water quality, freshwater biologists use naucorids as indicator species when monitoring rivers and wetlands.

sections.heading: One Last Thing
sections.body: The species illustrated here, Laccocoris hoogstraali, is named in honour of Harold Hoogstraal, an American parasitologist known for his work on ticks, reflecting the entomological tradition of commemorating colleagues in scientific names.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Stick insects (order Phasmatodea) are a worldwide group of over 3,600 known species whose slender bodies and thin legs let them pass as twigs, as seen in a specimen photographed among Acacia thorns in Kenya. The genus most likely responsible for this Acacia camouflage in East Africa is Bactrododema, large spiny stick insects formerly classified under the name Palophus before that name was folded into Bactrododema in 2005, though some databases still disagree on the correct name.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Stick insects have long cylindrical bodies, thin legs, and usually reduced or absent wings, with simple chewing mouthparts and long thread-like antennae, and their main defence is simply not being seen. In one newly described southern African species, Macynia mcgregororum, females (73-84 mm) are noticeably larger than males (57-64 mm) and carry pale bumpy tubercles the males lack; some species also carry internal chemical-spray glands that CT scans show vary greatly in size and shape across the order.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: Stick insects develop through a simple egg-nymph-adult life cycle without a caterpillar stage or cocoon, and in several species females can reproduce without mating, as in the well-studied Indian walking stick, whose eggs take 10-12 weeks to hatch. All stick insects are strict plant-eaters, and the Acacia-associated genus Bactrododema appears to feed specifically on Acacia foliage, though the underlying diet research was behind a paywall and so is noted as well-supported but not fully double-checked.

sections.heading: The Ultimate Game of Pretend
sections.body: Beyond looking like a stick, many species sway gently to mimic a twig moving in the wind, and if grabbed by a predator, some can snap off a trapped leg at a weak point to escape, later regrowing it slightly smaller than before. Some species also release a foul-smelling chemical spray from thoracic glands when threatened.

sections.heading: A Kenyan Detective Story
sections.body: Museum specimens of Bactrododema collected near Lake Turkana in 1905 and Taveta in 1912 are echoed by modern iNaturalist sightings of the same genus in Laikipia and Narok counties in 2024, with other Kenyan records spanning Mount Elgon, Kitale, Isiolo, Tsavo, Amboseli, and the coast near Kilifi and Kwale. This suggests these camouflaged insects have persisted across a wide stretch of Kenya for over a century, largely unnoticed.

sections.heading: Are They Pests? Are They Useful?
sections.body: Available scientific literature shows no evidence of stick insects being pests in Kenya or anywhere in Africa, unlike well-documented outbreaks elsewhere such as North America, Australia, Pacific islands, China, Colombia, and India. The only African mention found was an introduced pet-trade species causing a minor nuisance in South African gardens, though the report notes the absence of evidence may simply reflect a lack of study.

sections.heading: How Do People Deal With Outbreaks (Elsewhere)?
sections.body: Where stick insects have become pests outside Africa, control methods have included parasitic wasps and flies, general predators, insecticides (some now recognised as environmentally harmful and largely abandoned), sticky trunk bands, smoking palm fronds, and clearing ground litter to expose eggs. For small-scale nuisances like an unwanted pet stick insect, the simplest approach is picking them off by hand and freezing any eggs for a week.

sections.heading: Notable Facts
sections.body: The first stick insect formally named in this African group, Palophus centaurus (now Bactrododema centaurum), was described from a specimen collected in Old Calabar, Nigeria, not East or southern Africa. The world's longest known insect overall is a stick insect, Chan's Megastick, whose type specimen is held at the Natural History Museum in London, and a regrown leg always emerges slightly smaller than the original, serving as a permanent record of an escaped predator attack.

sections.heading: What Is a Stout Backswimmer?
sections.body: The Stout Backswimmer (Enithares sobria) is a true bug in the order Hemiptera, family Notonectidae (the backswimmers), a worldwide family of roughly 350-400 freshwater species. The genus Enithares is an Old World group spanning Africa and Asia, and is the backswimmer most likely to be encountered at the water's edge in East Africa.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The body is broadly oval and strongly domed like an upturned boat hull, and the concave underside traps an air bubble for diving. Adults are 5-15 mm long, with wings lying flat in a tent-like arrangement and colouration ranging from pale cream to brown, orange, red, blue, or violet. The long, paddle-shaped, bristle-fringed hind legs work as oars, while the short front and middle legs grasp prey; nymphs look like wingless miniature adults and pass through five moults, skipping a pupal stage.

sections.heading: The Upside-Down Life
sections.body: Backswimmers are unusual among swimming animals in that they swim belly-up, a position driven by the buoyant air bubble held against the underside by water-repelling hairs. The bubble also works as an underwater lung, since oxygen from the surrounding water diffuses in to replace what is used, extending dive time. At rest the insect hangs at roughly a 30-degree angle at the surface, ready to dive or take flight, and backswimmers often disperse at night to colonise new ponds.

sections.heading: A Ferocious Hunter
sections.body: Backswimmers are top invertebrate predators that hunt mosquito larvae, water fleas, small crustaceans, other aquatic insect larvae and pupae, and occasionally newly hatched fish, seizing prey with their front legs and injecting digestive saliva through a needle-like beak. They genuinely reduce mosquito populations, and female mosquitoes may avoid laying eggs in infested ponds, though control is patchy since the insects eat whatever prey is most abundant. Studies of optimal foraging show backswimmers match the theoretical ideal for allocating time between food-rich and food-poor patches.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Backswimmers inhabit still or slow-moving freshwater worldwide, including ponds, lakes, marshes, rice paddies, and slow streams, with a strong preference for water with emergent vegetation. Because they fly readily and are drawn to light at night, they are often among the first insects to colonise a new pond, sometimes within days of it filling.

sections.heading: Do They Bite?
sections.body: Yes, and painfully — the beak built for piercing aquatic prey pierces fingers just as easily, which is why Germans call them 'water-bees' and the British once called them 'boat flies' or 'wherrymen.' They are not aggressive toward humans but will bite in self-defence, making backswimmers that colonise swimming pools a particular nuisance.

sections.heading: Are They Important?
sections.body: In the freshwater food web backswimmers suppress invertebrate populations including mosquito larvae, serve as prey for fish and wading birds, and act as indicators of healthy, well-oxygenated water. They can be a nuisance in fish hatcheries by preying on newly hatched fish, and in parts of Mexico people harvest the eggs and adults of related Notonecta species as food, eating the eggs directly and grinding dried adults into flour.

sections.heading: How Are They Collected?
sections.body: Backswimmers are collected with an aquatic net swept through vegetation, since they float at the surface and submerge when disturbed. Adults that fly at night can also be taken at light traps near water; adults are preserved as dry pins through the centre of the thorax, while nymphs are stored in 80% alcohol.

sections.heading: Are They Really Giant Mosquitoes?
sections.body: Crane flies are not mosquitoes; they belong to the family Tipulidae, and adults cannot bite because their mouthparts are absent or reduced to stubs, with most adults never eating before dying within a few days of emerging. Tiger crane flies, genus Nephrotoma, belong to the same family as roughly 15,000 other crane fly species, making Tipulidae the largest fly family on Earth; entomologist Charles P. Alexander alone described more than 10,000 of those species.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like Up Close?
sections.body: The orange-and-black 'tiger' banding is striking under magnification, and the large dark compound eyes are of an unusual 'acone' type lacking an internal lens, otherwise found mainly in Hemiptera. The antennae are jet-black and comb-like, unlike the simple bristle or knob antennae of most flies, and a long rostrum projects from the head even though the mouthparts behind it are non-functional. The halteres (balance organs behind the wings) are proportionally much larger than in other flies, exceeding 12% of wing length.

sections.heading: What Are the Larvae Doing Under Your Lawn?
sections.body: The larvae, called leatherjackets, are tough-skinned, worm-like burrowers with a retracted head that live in soil, waterlogged moss, submerged leaf packs, rotting wood, or even rocky intertidal shorelines, with some species reaching 55 mm. A close relative, Tipula flaveolineata, has independently evolved a hindgut fermentation chamber like that of scarab beetles, packed with bacteria that break down plant cell walls most animals cannot digest.

sections.heading: How Do They Find Each Other?
sections.body: Adult crane flies live only a few days, and males of many species form swarms of up to thousands above a fixed ground marker to attract females. In Tipula oleracea, courtship involves a rigid, ordered sequence of leg-stroking movements the female abandons if performed out of order, and larvae of Tipula simplex release an aggregation pheromone in their feces that draws other larvae to shared shelter.

sections.heading: Why Don't Predators Eat Them Easily?
sections.body: Many crane flies, including tiger crane flies, are Batesian mimics whose orange-and-black banding resembles the warning colours of stinging wasps and hornets, deterring predators despite the fly being harmless. Their long legs are also deliberately expendable through autotomy, detaching cleanly if grabbed so the fly can escape, and the tough leatherjacket skin makes larvae unpalatable compared with a soft caterpillar.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter in the Wild?
sections.body: Crane fly larvae are primary shredders in streams, chewing fallen leaves into smaller pieces that release nutrients for other animals, and without them whole stream food chains would suffer. Tipula abdominalis strongly prefers hickory, maple, and chestnut leaves over beech and oak, growing faster on its preferred diet simply by eating more of it. Adult crane flies are also an important food source for birds, bats, fish, and amphibians, notably fuelling migrating birds during mass emergences in the UK.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Tiger crane flies occur worldwide from tropical forests to the Mediterranean, where 72% of local Tipulidae species are found nowhere else, to the High Arctic. Some Arctic relatives have reduced or absent wings — the wingless genus Chionea is active on snowfields in winter — while a handful of other crane fly species live in marine intertidal zones among algae and barnacles.

sections.heading: Are They Pests?
sections.body: Larvae of some crane fly species, notably the European crane fly Tipula paludosa, can reach damaging densities in pastures, golf courses, and lawns, and soil nematodes have proven effective as a pesticide-free biological control. Tiger crane flies (Nephrotoma) themselves are not known as significant crop pests and are predominantly woodland and meadow insects.

sections.heading: A Parting Thought
sections.body: Tipulidae fossils from 93 million years ago are virtually indistinguishable from living crane flies, meaning the tiger crane fly's lineage predates the diversification of the dinosaurs. Despite spreading into 15,000 species across every habitat from snowfields to seashores, crane flies remain delicate, long-legged, harmless animals whose adult lives last only a few days.

sections.heading: What Are Stoneflies?
sections.body: Stoneflies are ancient aquatic insects whose lineage stretches back over 250 million years to the Permian period, predating the dinosaurs. About 3,500 species have been described, but scientists estimate the true total is closer to 7,000, meaning roughly half of all stonefly species remain unknown. True stoneflies (family Perlidae) are well-represented in the tropics, and the genus Neoperla is one of the dominant stonefly groups in tropical Africa and Southeast Asia.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults are flat, brownish insects with two pairs of wings folded flat over the back, long thread-like antennae, and short paired tails called cerci. Nymphs live entirely underwater, resemble wingless miniature adults, and sprawl on the undersides of rocks in fast-flowing streams using strong, hairy legs. Neoperla nymphs are predators with strong mouthparts, and unlike many other stonefly relatives they lack abdominal gill tufts, absorbing oxygen through their skin and small thoracic gill structures instead.

sections.heading: A Remarkable Life in Two Worlds
sections.body: Females lay eggs on or above the water surface that sink to the streambed, and the nymphs that hatch spend one to three years or longer living under rocks in cold, fast-flowing streams, including highland streams draining Mount Kenya and the Aberdares. They moult through up to 22 growth stages before emerging as winged adults, and most adults do not eat at all, living just one to four weeks to find a mate before dying.

sections.heading: Love Songs in Vibration
sections.body: Males cannot produce conventional sound, so they drum the substrate with the abdomen tip to send species-specific vibrations through rock or log, and receptive females drum back so the pair can locate each other. This drumming courtship is found only in the stonefly group that includes Neoperla, and the vibration-sensing organs that detect it are located inside the insects' legs.

sections.heading: Why Clean Water Matters to Them — and to Us
sections.body: Stonefly nymphs require cold, clean, well-oxygenated water with rocky beds and are driven out by pollution, siltation, or warming, making them one of the most widely used indicators of river health worldwide, including in monitoring programmes across Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the EU, the UK, the US, and East Africa. As predators the Neoperla group keeps smaller invertebrate populations in check, and as prey stonefly nymphs are a staple food for trout, salmon, and other freshwater fish.

sections.heading: Under Threat
sections.body: In the United States 43% of stonefly species are classified as at risk of extinction, and losses in tropical regions may be going undetected because most tropical species have never even been described. Main threats include deforestation, dams, mining, livestock grazing, road construction, and climate change, since stoneflies are cold-water specialists; a Tasmanian study found that removing streamside forest buffers caused stonefly numbers to drop by 34%.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Water boatmen belong to the family Corixidae, true bugs with piercing, sucking mouthparts related to shield bugs, assassin bugs, and bed bugs, with over 600 species worldwide making Corixidae the most diverse family of aquatic bugs. The genus Sigara is the largest in the family, occurs worldwide, and is the one most likely encountered in a typical pond; the Aztecs named them axayacatl, 'seeds of the water.'

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: A water boatman is an oval, flattened, mottled brown insect roughly 5-15 mm long, camouflaged against gravelly bottoms and weed beds. The long, hair-fringed hind legs row like oars, the middle legs anchor the insect to plant stems, and the front legs are flattened into a unique single-segment scoop called the pala used to shovel food into the mouth. The short, unsegmented beak (rostrum) is another diagnostic feature found in no other true bug family.

sections.heading: How Do They Breathe?
sections.body: Before submerging, a water boatman traps an air bubble beneath its wing cases that functions as a physical gill, with oxygen diffusing in from the surrounding water to extend dive time until the bubble shrinks and the insect must resurface. The male's abdominal strigil was long assumed to be a sound-producing organ, but it is actually used for gripping the female during mating and for managing the air bubble.

sections.heading: What Do They Eat?
sections.body: Unlike most predatory true bugs, water boatmen are largely vegetarian, scooping up algae, diatoms, and decaying plant material with the pala and dissolving it with saliva before drawing it in through the straw-like mouthpart. Some species are more flexible and also eat mosquito larvae, tiny shrimp, and other small animals, but algae and detritus form the bulk of the diet, making them peaceful grazers among the pond's assassins.

sections.heading: The Loudest Animal on Earth (Relative to Size)
sections.body: Male water boatmen sing to attract females by rubbing the penis against the abdomen, producing a chirp that, relative to body size, is louder than any other sound produced by any animal, audible from a metre away despite the insect's 2 mm size. The sound is produced underwater and is mostly inaudible at the surface; the stridulation mechanism has been confirmed by scientific study since the 1970s, giving water boatmen a legitimate world record as the loudest animal on Earth by body-size ratio.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Water boatmen live in almost any still or slow-moving fresh water, including ponds, lake margins, drainage ditches, rice paddies, and slow streams, and some species tolerate brackish or saline pools where few other insects survive. Many species are powerful fliers that relocate when a pond dries up or freezes, often turning up en masse at outdoor lights at night.

sections.heading: Do People Eat Them?
sections.body: Adults are eaten in Mexico and Egypt, described as tasting 'slightly crablike,' and can be roasted, fried, or boiled. Their tiny eggs, known in Mexico as ahuahutle, were harvested as a staple food long before the Spanish arrived by anchoring twig bundles in shallow lakes for the insects to lay eggs on; the 16th-century historian Sahagun recorded that Emperor Montezuma had runners sprint fresh eggs 25 kilometres from Lake Texcoco to his table for breakfast. The eggs are still sold today in the international pet-food trade.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: As primary consumers of algae and organic detritus, water boatmen convert plant material into animal flesh that is then eaten by fish, frogs, waterfowl, and larger predatory insects, so removing them shortens the food web significantly. They are also a model system in ecology: 1970s research found that twelve species can coexist in the same pond through temporal niche partitioning, breeding at different times of year, and further work showed species can coexist even under strong, unequal competition.

sections.heading: One More Surprising Thing
sections.body: Water boatmen are sometimes confused with the backswimmer, a superficially similar bug that swims upside-down and can deliver a painful bite, but the water boatman swims right-side up, is largely harmless, and will not bite. If scooped into a jar of water it will row steadily to the surface, refill its air bubble, and dive back down.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: The water-penny larva is a flat, oval disc barely a few millimetres across, pressed tightly against a rock in a fast, clean stream, and East Africa's own water-penny beetles belong to the genus Afrobrianax, found in streams flowing from Mount Kenya and the Aberdares. Water-penny beetles belong to the family Psephenidae, part of the same insect order as ladybirds, dung beetles, and fireflies, but specialised for life in cold, oxygen-rich, rocky streams.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The larva is almost perfectly flat, oval, and disc-like, with legs splaying outward from its sides rather than hanging beneath it, giving it the look of a tiny armoured, scalloped shield under a hand lens. This flatness lets it live within the 'boundary layer' of nearly still water — only a millimetre or two thick — that forms against any hard surface in fast-flowing water, so it disappears beneath the torrent rather than fighting it. Adults, by contrast, look like ordinary small brown beetles.

sections.heading: An Extraordinary Breathing System
sections.body: Unlike most aquatic insects, which must leave the water to pupate, some water-penny beetle species pupate underwater using spiracular gills — branching filaments sprouting from the abdominal breathing pores. In one species, Psephenoides gahani, these gills have roughly 40 hollow branches braced by microscopic cuticular struts, working like a physical gill that draws dissolved oxygen from the water. Unlike most comparable insect structures, which rely on internal fluid pressure to keep their shape, these gills are rigid, so they keep functioning regardless of the insect's hydration state; even the larvae have cuticular modifications around their breathing pores that let them pull oxygen from the water without breaking the surface.

sections.heading: Life in Fast Water
sections.body: Water-penny larvae are grazers that scrape the thin film of algae and organic material (periphyton) from stones in fast-flowing streams, functioning like very slow, very flat lawnmowers. Because periphyton-covered boulders in fast, rocky streams signal clean, well-oxygenated water, the presence of water-penny larvae is associated with stream health.

sections.heading: Why They Matter
sections.body: Water-penny beetles combine physics and biology: their flat larvae exploit fluid dynamics near surfaces rather than brute force, and their pupal spiracular gills are among the most complex respiratory structures found in any beetle pupa. For the African genus Afrobrianax specifically, the entomological literature consulted for this report has no direct information; what is known from family-wide research points to a group of stream-dwelling beetles that are both ecologically specialised and physiologically innovative.

sections.heading: What Are Water Scavenger Beetles?
sections.body: Water scavenger beetles look at a glance like diving beetles — streamlined, oval, shiny black — but the long feelers on the head are not antennae; they are elongated mouthpart feelers called maxillary palps that mimic antennae, while the real antennae are short, clubbed, and tucked away. They belong to the family Hydrophilidae, with roughly 2,800 described species in about 170 genera found on every continent except Antarctica, ranging from a few millimetres to giants over 40 mm long.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults are typically oval, strongly domed, jet black, and polished on top, while the underside carries a dense mat of water-repelling hairs that trap a thin air film (a plastron) acting as an underwater gill. The larvae look nothing like the adults: they are elongated, flattened, and fierce, with an unusual upward-facing head and syringe-like mouthparts that inject digestive juices into prey. One group, the genus Berosus, has independently evolved lateral abdominal gills almost identical to those of unrelated mayfly larvae.

sections.heading: Strange Engineering and Surprising Behaviour
sections.body: Females spin a silken egg case with a mast-like snorkel that aerates the eggs while the case floats or is anchored to a leaf, and in one subfamily (Epimetopinae) the female carries the case attached to her own abdomen until the eggs hatch, after which females of many species stand guard over eggs and young larvae. Despite their aquatic lives, adults are poor swimmers that row with alternate legs rather than the coordinated strokes of diving beetles, so they mostly crawl rather than swim; the larvae of Hydrobius fuscipes instead skate across the underside of the water surface using body undulations, with their tracheal gills acting as suction anchors. Like all beetles they undergo complete metamorphosis, but the larvae must leave the water and burrow into damp soil to pupate before returning to the water as adults.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Most water scavenger beetles live in still or slow-moving fresh water such as ponds, marshes, flooded rice paddies, and stream edges, and adults are drawn to artificial lights at night, sometimes turning up in outdoor swimming pools and occasionally biting swimmers. One entire subfamily, the Sphaeridiinae, has abandoned aquatic life altogether and lives in dung, compost, and decaying leaf litter despite looking almost identical to its aquatic cousins.

sections.heading: What Do They Eat?
sections.body: Adults are primarily scavengers on algae, decaying plant material, and organic debris, though larger species will also attack live invertebrates and even tiny fish. Larvae, by contrast, are committed predators from the moment they hatch, hunting other aquatic insects, small crustaceans, and anything they can overpower — a split in diet that lets the two generations avoid competing for food.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Hydrophilidae became an early test case for DNA barcoding, with a study confirming the method accurately separates species in the family and even uncovers previously unknown species hidden within known ones. The dung-dwelling Sphaeridiinae have also attracted interest as biological control agents, since their larvae prey on the eggs and young larvae of dung-breeding flies that spread disease and irritate livestock, prompting Australian researchers to investigate importing South African dung beetles from this group.

sections.heading: How Are They Found and Collected?
sections.body: The standard collecting method is an aquatic net with a fine mesh on a D-shaped or round frame, swept through aquatic vegetation, leaf litter, and substrate. Adults attracted to lights can also be collected at light traps at night, and the swimming-pool habit of some species means they occasionally arrive uninvited and can be scooped out by hand.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Water scorpions are true bugs in the order Hemiptera, family Nepidae, a group of around 268 species found mainly in tropical and subtropical freshwater habitats worldwide. The genus Laccotrephes is widespread across South and South-East Asia and China, while the stick-insect-like Ranatra and the broad, flat Nepa occur much more widely, including Europe and the Americas. Despite the name, they are not scorpions and cannot sting — the 'tail' is a breathing tube, not a stinger.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The long, slender rear projection is a snorkel-like breathing tube, not a sting, with its breathing openings (spiracles) unusually located at the base rather than the tip, so air drawn in at the surface must travel the tube's full length to reach the body. The forelegs are powerful and raptorial, folding like a penknife to grip prey, while the long, spindly middle and hind legs are used for clinging to vegetation rather than swimming. Body colour is a uniform dull brown for camouflage; Laccotrephes is oval-bodied and squat while Ranatra resembles a water-walking stick insect, and both can reach 30-45 mm in body length excluding the breathing tube.

sections.heading: How Do They Hunt?
sections.body: Water scorpions are patient sit-and-wait predators that hang motionless among underwater plants or debris with only the tip of the breathing tube breaking the surface, then shoot out their raptorial forelegs to seize prey that comes close enough. Like all true bugs they feed by stabbing a sharp beak into the prey and sucking out the body fluids, taking mosquito larvae, small crustaceans, aquatic insect nymphs, and occasionally tiny fish or tadpoles; Ranatra nymphs have been recorded eating up to 33 mosquito larvae per hour in the laboratory. The bite is painful if a water scorpion is picked up.

sections.heading: What Is Their Life Cycle?
sections.body: Water scorpions develop by incomplete metamorphosis, hatching as miniature nymphs that moult through a series of stages without a pupal stage. Laccotrephes females lay around 100 eggs over a season at roughly 1-2 per day, often in two batches; eggs hatch in 12-13 days and the five nymphal stages are completed in about 40 days, with adults and nymphs of many species able to overwinter. In Nepa, each egg carries seven delicate filaments for gas exchange while buried in waterlogged plant material without any parental help, unlike the related giant water bugs (Lethocerus), whose males carry the eggs on their backs.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live?
sections.body: Water scorpions favour still or slow-moving freshwater such as ponds, ditches, marshes, flooded rice paddies, and garden water features, preferring shallow, weedy water where they can cling to vegetation and reach the surface with their breathing tube; they are unlikely to be found in fast-running streams. They occur across most of the tropics and subtropics, with Laccotrephes especially common from India to Japan, and despite having fully formed wings they rarely fly, so isolated pond populations can remain cut off from one another for long periods.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: As mid-level predators, water scorpions help keep populations of smaller invertebrates in check, and their preference for mosquito larvae makes them genuinely useful — Laccotrephes grossus and the closely related L. maculatus have been studied as potential biocontrol agents for mosquitoes in Asia. On the downside, large water scorpions in fish-farm ponds can prey on juvenile fish, occasionally becoming a nuisance to aquaculture.

sections.heading: How Are They Collected?
sections.body: A simple aquatic dip net swept through pond vegetation and leaf litter is enough to collect them, though because water scorpions stay completely still rather than swim away when disturbed, careful inspection of the net contents is needed to spot them. They can be kept in still-water aquaria and will accept live prey.

sections.heading: Anything Surprising?
