sections.body: Ranatra produces sound underwater by rubbing its front leg against its body, suggesting these insects communicate acoustically in a medium rarely associated with insect song. Their fossil relatives were already swimming through Jurassic ponds 180 million years ago, long before flowering plants appeared, and while the closely related giant water bug (Lethocerus) is eaten as a delicacy across South-East Asia, water scorpions seem to have escaped that fate entirely.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: A wheel bug (Arilus cristatus) is one of the largest and most fearsome true bugs in North America, a member of the ambush-and-puncture assassin bug family (Reduviidae). It stabs prey with a needle-like beak, injects a fluid that liquefies the victim's insides within seconds, and drinks the results. The typical photo of one shows a nymph, not an adult: nymphs are bright orange-red with black spines, quite unlike the drab grey-brown adult.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults reach about an inch and a half long, dark grey-brown, with a distinctive semicircular crest of 8 to 12 tooth-like points on the back that gives the species its name — its actual purpose (defense, mating, or something else) is still an open question. Nymphs lack the wheel entirely (it only forms at the final adult molt) and instead wear red-and-black warning colors through five nymphal stages. Eggs are laid upright in tight hexagonal, honeycomb-like clusters cemented with a natural glue.

sections.heading: How Does It Hunt?
sections.body: The wheel bug is a patient ambush predator that waits on a leaf or twig, grabs passing prey with its front legs, and injects a digestive saliva that begins dissolving the victim's insides within 15 to 30 seconds before it drinks the liquefied meal. One documented nymph consumed 69 adult and 22 larval Mexican bean beetles in under a month.

sections.heading: Why Should You Be Careful?
sections.body: A wheel bug's bite works on human skin too and is described as roughly ten times worse than a bee sting, with burning pain and numbness that can last days. A 1920s medical case described a girl bitten twice on the finger who developed small horn-like growths at the puncture sites that took months to disappear, with the finger staying noticeably warmer for a year afterward. It isn't dangerous like a scorpion sting, but admiration from a distance is recommended.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Wheel bugs are a New World species found across the southern and eastern United States, into Mexico and as far south as Guatemala; over 41,000 confirmed sightings exist with none from Africa, so the species has never been recorded in Kenya. Kenya does have close relatives in the same subfamily, though: assassin bugs Scipinnia repax and a Nagusta species studied near Mbita Point on Lake Victoria that specialize in hunting jumping spiders, plus a separate newly described assassin bug species from Tanzania.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: In their native range, wheel bugs are valued for preying on caterpillars, pest beetles, and the invasive brown marmorated stink bug, though they also eat beneficial insects like ladybugs and honeybees indiscriminately. Nobody has turned the wheel bug into a commercial pest-control product; its usefulness is incidental.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: Wheel bugs can produce a small chirping sound by rubbing the beak against ridged grooves on the chest, though nobody is sure of its purpose. They live one generation per year, overwintering as eggs, hatching in spring, passing through five nymphal stages by summer, and laying a fresh batch of eggs on bark or twigs in the fall.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: The wheel bug is an ambush hunter with a mysterious cogwheel crest, capable of one of the most painful stings among North American insects, yet broadly beneficial to gardeners. It has no presence in East Africa, but its close relatives in Kenya show the same ruthless hunting instincts.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Whirligig beetles are small, shiny beetles seen whirling in circles on still pond surfaces, belonging to the family Gyrinidae — roughly 700 species found in freshwater worldwide. The genus Dineutus (also spelled Dineutes) contains some of the largest and most impressive species, with an iridescent, jewel-like gleam.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: An adult is compact, oval, and streamlined, with a water-repelling dome-shaped shell on top and an underside wetted by the surface film, living exactly at the air-water boundary. Its most extraordinary feature is eyes split in half, watching the sky above and the water below simultaneously. Broad, paddle-like middle and hind legs fringed with cuticular blades let it reach speeds of 55 centimetres per second and spin at up to 12 rotations per second.

sections.heading: How Do They Sense the World?
sections.body: Whirligig beetles navigate by generating tiny ripples as they skim the surface, then detecting the ripples that bounce back off obstacles through an internal vibration sensor in the antennae called Johnston's organ. They process the direction and timing of returning ripples fast enough to steer clear of collisions — effectively echolocation using waves on water instead of sound in air.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: Adults hunt at the water's surface, taking any struggling insect that falls in, such as flies, moths, or small spiders. Larvae are an entirely different, bottom-dwelling story: hidden, slow-moving predators with feathery gills for underwater breathing, occupying a different ecological niche from the adults in the same pond.

sections.heading: How Do They Defend Themselves?
sections.body: Speed and unpredictable spinning are the first defence against fish. If seized, adults release gyrinidal, a deterrent and likely toxic compound, making them an unpleasant mouthful. Even pupae aren't fully safe — certain bombardier beetles have learned to parasitise gyrinid pupae.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Whirligig beetles prey on surface-film insects including mosquitoes and midges, while their larvae consume bottom-dwelling invertebrates, linking surface and benthic food webs in the same pond. Engineers designing small autonomous aquatic robots have studied their swimming mechanics, paddle design, and ripple-based sensing. In parts of East Africa, whirligig beetles (together with diving beetles) are collected by hand and held against the skin, where their defensive secretions are believed in traditional practice to have medicinal effects.

sections.heading: The Bigger Picture
sections.body: A whirligig beetle sees two worlds at once, senses via waves on water, swims faster than almost any invertebrate its size, and carries deterrent chemistry — and has done so in essentially the same form since the Jurassic period.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Aedes is a huge genus of mosquitoes — nearly 1,000 species found on every continent except Antarctica — including Aedes aegypti (the yellow fever mosquito) and Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito), which together spread dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever to hundreds of millions of people yearly. Genetic studies have found that the roughly 932 species lumped under 'Aedes' don't all share one common ancestor, meaning the genus as currently defined isn't a single clean lineage, and untangling it is ongoing work.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Aedes mosquitoes have narrow, dark bodies with sharp black-and-white or silver scale patterns, especially pronounced in the striped Ae. albopictus ('tiger mosquito'). Wing length changes with rearing temperature — wings grown at 15°C were around 30% longer than those grown at 35°C. Yellow fever mosquitoes exist as a pale, city-loving form and a darker wild form that interbreed so freely (over 40% of family groups in one Senegal study contained both) that they're now considered one flexible species rather than two.

sections.heading: How Do They Feed and Breed?
sections.body: Females need blood to make eggs and favor laying them in small man-made water containers — buckets, flowerpots, gutters, and especially old tires, which accounted for over 85% of larval sites in one Cameroon survey. Ae. aegypti bites and lays eggs most eagerly around 30°C, while the cooler-climate Ae. albopictus peaks around 25°C.

sections.heading: Growing Up — From Egg to Adult
sections.body: Like all mosquitoes, Aedes passes through egg, larva, pupa, and adult stages, with the journey from egg to flying adult taking as little as 7 to 10 days under good conditions. In a narrow two-hour window roughly 11 to 13 hours after being laid, the egg builds a tough chitin-armored coating (serosal cuticle) that lets it survive months of drying out and still hatch once wetted — a trait suited to the temporary puddles Aedes favors.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Aedes mosquitoes are found nearly worldwide except Antarctica, but the two star species behave differently within that range: in a Cameroon survey, the yellow fever mosquito was found everywhere researchers looked, while the Asian tiger mosquito was confined to the wetter south. Genetic fingerprinting there found nearly 80% of tiger mosquitoes shared the same genetic signature, consistent with a recent, rapidly spreading founder population.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Aedes aegypti is the world's primary dengue carrier; reported global cases climbed from about half a million in 2000 to a record 14.6 million in 2024, likely an undercount. Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever ride the same mosquitoes, which stay infectious for life once infected and can pick up a virus from a person before that person feels sick.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: One taxonomic study scored 172 physical features across every life stage of 119 species, leading scientists to split Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus into their own genus, Stegomyia, for a time, though many still call them Aedes. The egg's drought-survival switch flips in a precise two-hour window (hour 11 to 13), and old tire piles left in the rain can be among the most productive mosquito nurseries in a landscape.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: Aedes mosquitoes are a sprawling, still-being-sorted-out group whose two most famous members have turned old tires and rain puddles into launch pads for fast-growing infectious diseases. Their drought-proof eggs and knack for exploiting man-made puddles make them formidable, adaptable survivors and a persistent public health challenge.

sections.heading: What Is It?
sections.body: The armoured katydid (Acanthoplus discoidalis, per the online-sourced report) is a heavy, spiny, flightless cricket relative from the grasslands of southern Africa, known as koringkriek ('corn cricket') in Afrikaans and Setotojane to farmers in the region. It sits in a small African branch, Hetrodinae, within the katydid family Tettigoniidae. Its most dramatic trait is a deliberate defence: when attacked, it can squirt its own blood at the threat.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults are about 5 centimetres long, wide-bodied and heavy for an insect, colored brown, green, black, or reddish, with a hard, spiky exoskeleton and a shield-like plate (pronotum) over the back that gives the species its 'armoured' name. It is flightless, probably never travelling more than a few kilometres in its life, has powerful jaws capable of a painful nip, and its large body mass means it must actively shuffle around bushes to manage its temperature.

sections.heading: A Family Tree Surprise
sections.body: A DNA-based study using specimens from Namibia, Zambia, and South Africa found this African group to be a true single branch (monophyletic) on the katydid family tree. Its closest relative is another African shieldback katydid group, so close that it's a live open question whether that group should be folded into the armoured katydid's own branch.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: Females bury egg pods of 6 to 12 eggs a couple of centimetres into soil, preferring dry, loose soil under Acacia trees over crop fields; roughly half of all eggs laid are eaten by underground ants, and an egg can wait 8 to 12 months before hatching. Hatchlings are miniature wingless versions of adults that take two to three months to grow up, and adults are opportunistic omnivores eating grass and cereal heads as well as scavenged carrion, other insects, or bird nestlings. Males transfer a nutritious mating gift weighing up to a fifth of their body weight, which the female eats; a female can store sperm to lay multiple egg batches without remating.

sections.heading: Why Does It Bleed on Purpose?
sections.body: When grabbed, the cricket can rupture seams in its leg joints and squirt foul-smelling, distasteful blood (hemolymph) at a threat, sometimes several centimetres; about six in ten leg-attacks triggered this in lab tests, and the blood put off reptile predators in feeding trials. It may also bite, spit up stomach contents, or (males only) buzz a rasping alarm sound, layering several defences at once.

sections.heading: Is It a Pest?
sections.body: The two underlying reports disagree on how confirmed this is: book-sourced literature says it has only a folk reputation as a cornfield pest in southern Africa, with no book directly documenting the connection. Online-sourced field research states it definitively, calling it the single worst pest of grain crops in northern Namibia and the second-worst in eastern Botswana, with outbreaks wiping out 30-40% of a region's sorghum or millet harvest. Outbreaks are local population explosions rather than migrating swarms, since the insect is flightless.

sections.heading: How Do Farmers Fight Back?
sections.body: A baited trench — a ditch dug around a field with insecticide mixed into cereal bran — killed over 90% of crickets crossing it within a day, far better than an unbaited trench, and a modified animal-drawn plough cutting a steep furrow blocked about 30% of crickets unaided. This targeted, edge-only approach was gentler on other insect life than broadcast spraying, which caused lasting damage across almost every insect group checked.

sections.heading: Would You Eat It?
sections.body: Katydids and relatives are eaten across Africa generally (insect protein converts feed far more efficiently than livestock), and with growing interest in insects as protein, researchers have begun looking at these crickets as a food source for animals and people — though farmers reportedly had to wash them carefully first since chickens sometimes refused to eat them with their defensive chemicals still on.

sections.heading: Notable Facts
sections.body: Chemicals released by ripening sorghum that attract this cricket belong to the same class desert locusts use to trigger swarming — a coincidence between two very different pests. Locally the cricket is enough of a well-known character that a farmer-outreach program built around fighting it had its own theme songs, poems, and a dedicated festival day.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: Click beetles are a family, Elateridae, likely holding over 10,000 species worldwide, named for their trick of righting themselves with an audible click when flipped onto their back. They belong to the beetle order Coleoptera, the largest group of animals on Earth, and are essentially tiny spring-loaded machines.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: Adults are long, narrow, and plain — usually brown, black, or grey — with a loosely hinged join between the front body section and the rest, ending in two backward-pointing spikes. Their larvae, called wireworms, are thin, hard, shiny, wire-like grubs that live underground and can take two to eleven years to mature depending on species.

sections.heading: How Does the 'Click' Trick Actually Work?
sections.body: A small peg on the beetle's underside locks into a matching ledge as it slowly bends its body, like cocking a crossbow; releasing it snaps the hinge straight in a fraction of a second, flinging the beetle upright and producing the click. A handful of tropical species glow continuously from body spots (unrelated to firefly flashing), and genetic studies show fireflies are actually nested within the click beetle family tree — essentially specialized click beetles that gave up clicking for glowing.

sections.heading: Where Are They Found?
sections.body: Click beetles live almost everywhere on land, with larvae thriving in agricultural soil, grassland, and forest litter. A survey of sub-Saharan Africa catalogued 945 species in 75 genera; in Kenya, confirmed sightings include the genus Tetralobus around Amboseli and the Maasai Mara, an Alaus species near Watamu, and other genera in the Taita Hills, Wasini Island, and Turkana — Kenya has the best-documented click-beetle records in East Africa, though still fewer than 1,500 confirmed sightings.

sections.heading: Why Do They Matter?
sections.body: Wireworm larvae are among the most damaging soil pests worldwide, chewing through roots, seeds, and tubers of crops like maize, potatoes, wheat, and sugarcane, and are hard to monitor or control because of their long underground lives. But some genera, especially the large Alaus ('eyed elater') click beetles, have predatory larvae that eat other pest beetles in rotting wood — one larva was recorded eating over 200 wood-boring grubs before maturing.

sections.heading: A Few Things Worth Knowing
sections.body: Genetic testing shows some wireworms thought to be a single species are actually several nearly identical 'hidden' species that split apart tens of thousands of years ago. The eyespots on an Alaus click beetle's back are a bluff meant to startle predators into thinking they face something bigger, and the beetle's signature click is primarily a defensive move — startle, right itself, and escape in one motion.

sections.heading: In Summary
sections.body: The click beetle's identity centers on a spring-loaded hinge that turns being flipped onto its back into a minor inconvenience. Above ground the adults are unassuming; below ground their long-lived larvae are both costly crop pests and, in some genera, quiet pest controllers.

sections.heading: What Are They?
sections.body: A crane fly is the large, spindly insect that blunders into lights on summer evenings, often mistaken for an oversized mosquito, but it is entirely harmless — its reduced mouthparts mean it cannot bite, sting, or feed at all. Adults live only a few days, mostly to find a mate, and belong to the family Tipulidae, the single largest fly family on Earth under the broadest count, with roughly 14,000 species found on every continent.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The adult is essentially a set of exceptionally long legs on a thin brown body; the legs break off easily at special joints, possibly helping the fly escape predators. Its halteres (balance organs) are proportionally the largest of any fly, exceeding 12% of forewing length versus about 6% in a mosquito, making crane flies unusually nimble fliers. Uniquely among flies, their eyes lack a light-focusing crystalline cone, and they retain a primitive adhesive foot pad (arolium) that all other flies have replaced.

sections.heading: The Hidden Life: Leatherjackets
sections.body: Soil-dwelling crane fly larvae, called leatherjackets, have thick, rubbery skin and spend months or years feeding on plant roots and organic matter underground. In British pastures and lawns, Tipula paludosa and Tipula oleracea are serious agricultural pests, and about 2,000 species of parasitic wasps have been recorded attacking Tipulidae. Aquatic larvae, by contrast, live in fast-flowing streams and are powerful wood processors — one study found them fragmenting over 90% of decayed alder wood in a stream within a year.

sections.heading: Breathing Underwater
sections.body: Aquatic larvae breathe via spiracles lined with water-repelling hairs that trap a thin air film, letting oxygen diffuse in and carbon dioxide out continuously without surfacing — the same principle as a diving beetle's air bubble, but built into the cuticle. Some species carry this further at the pupal stage, growing branching gill filaments that let them stay fully submerged while transforming from larva to adult.

sections.heading: Arctic Survivors
sections.body: In the High Arctic, crane flies are among the last insect families present; nearly a quarter of Arctic North American species have reduced or lost their wings, mostly in females, saving energy in a cold, windy climate while males typically keep full wings to find mates. Tipula carinifrons, at the northern edge of its range, abandons plant material entirely and grazes on cyanobacteria mats on the tundra.

sections.heading: A Surprising Social Life
sections.body: Crane flies mate in aerial swarms, loose male aggregations gathering above a landmark such as a rock or grass tuft. Females use the same landmark cues as males — in a lab experiment a lone female tracked an artificial swarm marker just as a swarming male would, suggesting both sexes share identical rules for finding mating sites.

sections.heading: Why They Matter
sections.body: Migratory Arctic-breeding waders — dunlins, sandpipers, phalaropes, turnstones, many of which winter along East Africa's Rift Valley lakes and coastal mudflats — time their Arctic arrival to the brief summer flush of Tipulidae and chironomid midges, without which they could not provision chicks fast enough. Crane fly larvae shred leaves, process soil, break down wood, and feed everything from parasitic wasps to Arctic sandpipers, making them significant if unglamorous recyclers.

sections.heading: What Is It, Really?
sections.body: The spider belongs to the genus Leucauge, nicknamed 'orchard orbweavers,' 'stretch spiders,' or 'long-jawed orb weavers,' with more than 160 species across the tropics and subtropics and at least nine species in Kenya. The exact species in a given photo cannot be confirmed since Leucauge species are usually told apart by microscopic genital structures; the best guess based on coloring is often Leucauge festiva, though this remains an educated guess rather than a certainty.

sections.heading: What Do They Look Like?
sections.body: The body is oval and elongated with a silvery-white abdomen (from microscopic guanine crystals in the skin), dark stripes, and a splash of reddish-orange near the front, with pale, thin, disproportionately long legs. It rests with its front two leg pairs stretched forward and its back pair stretched behind in a dramatic 'X' pose that, combined with its shape, camouflages it as a twig or blade of grass.

sections.heading: How Do They Live?
sections.body: Leucauge spiders molt while hanging from the center of their own web, often leaving the discarded shell tangled in the silk afterward. Courtship involves the male tapping, jerking, rocking, and twanging the web's silk in a specific sequence; a receptive female responds by opening and closing her fangs and tilting upward. Certain parasitic wasps sting a Leucauge spider and somehow induce it to build a simplified web to hold a wasp cocoon before killing it.

sections.heading: Where Do They Live — and Are They in Kenya?
sections.body: Yes, confidently: a major survey backed by the National Museums of Kenya and international partners documented over 800 spider species in Kenya, nine of them Leucauge. Leucauge festiva specifically is recorded from Nairobi and Moyale and across a wide swath of Africa from Ethiopia and Sudan to South Africa and Madagascar. Checking citizen-recorded iNaturalist sightings, scientists found some Kenyan Leucauge identifications didn't make biological sense — likely misidentifications.

sections.heading: Should You Worry About a Bite?
sections.body: No — long-jawed orbweavers like Leucauge have jaws built for grabbing prey, though their venom is not considered dangerous to people. Of the spiders that do pose a medical risk to humans (widow and recluse spiders), Leucauge isn't among them.

sections.heading: Friend of the Farmer — Sort Of
sections.body: Leucauge eats mosquitoes and other small flies caught in its web, generally acting as a farm ally. However, in Japanese greenhouse eggplant farms, a relative, Leucauge blanda, was found eating a beneficial predatory bug farmers had released to control whiteflies and aphids, since the spider can't distinguish 'good' from 'bad' prey caught in its web.

sections.heading: The Real Marvel: Weaving Together
sections.body: An individual Leucauge web is modest — roughly dinner-plate sized up to about a metre — built from strong 'dragline' silk for the frame and stretchier, gluey silk for the spiral, with some spiders rebuilding up to 90% of the web daily. Some Leucauge species build colonially, with individual webs stitched onto one shared silk scaffold over streams, larger spiders claiming the top spots; others build their webs into the framework of a much bigger Nephila (golden silk orb-weaver) web to save silk.
